walkthroughs.body_html:
Inorganic Chemistry — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Inorganic Chemistry brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Inorganic Chemistry.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Members of a homologous series share:
options: The same molecular mass
The same functional group and general formula
The same boiling point
The same number of isomers

mcqs.q: Can a single standard electrode potential be measured in isolation?
options: Each electrode has an absolute potential that can be measured directly with a voltmeter.
No — electrode potentials are RELATIVE values measured against a reference (the standard hydrogen electrode, defined as 0 V).
A coordination number of 4 always means square planar because complexes prefer to be flat.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.

mcqs.q: If a complex ion has a coordination number of 4, what shape does it have?
options: A coordination number of 4 always means square planar because complexes prefer to be flat.
It can be either tetrahedral OR square planar — the shape depends on the metal and ligands (e.g. [Pt(NH3)4]2+ is square planar; [CuCl4]2- is tetrahedral).
A coordination number of 4 always means tetrahedral, because that gives the maximum bond-angle separation.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.

mcqs.q: If a reaction has a negative Gibbs free energy change, what does that mean?
options: A reaction with negative delta G will always happen quickly.
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — it can proceed — but it may still be very slow.
